title: Explicit block encodings of rate matrices for simulating polymerization kinetics on quantum computers
authors: Yuhei Ikeda, Hokuto Iwakiri, Soichiro Nishio, Kentaro Matsumoto
abstract: Predicting how molecular weight distribution and monomer sequence evolve during polymerization is central to polymer science, yet classical approaches face a trade-off between molecular resolution and computational cost: for copolymers, the number of distinguishable species grows exponentially with chain length. Quantum computing offers a potential alternative, provided the non-unitary rate matrices governing the kinetics can be embedded into unitary quantum circuits, a task known as block encoding. Here we construct explicit block-encoding circuits for two kinetic models of living polymerization: Model A, single-monomer polymerization, whose lower-bidiagonal rate matrix is encoded via a sparse-oracle construction and a two-term linear combination of unitaries (LCU) decomposition; and Model B, two-monomer copolymerization, where a bijective labeling of polymer species by an integer index (the m-index) yields a structured sparse matrix encoded via either a five-term LCU or a sparse-oracle construction. Numerical simulations with the sparse-oracle encodings reproduce the classical time evolution for reactivity ratios drawn from reported olefin copolymerization systems spanning near-random ($r_1 r_2 \simeq 1$) and blocky ($r_1 r_2 > 1$) microstructures, and the LCU encodings are verified by explicit reconstruction of the encoded matrix block. Resource estimation shows that both implementations require only $O(\log N)$ qubits in the matrix dimension $N$ (an exponential memory saving over the classical state space), with gate counts growing gradually, reaching $10^4$ to $10^5$ gates at $10^3$ system qubits. These results establish a concrete quantum circuit foundation for simulating polymerization kinetics on fault-tolerant quantum hardware, and a first step toward exploiting exponential state-space compression for high-dimensional polymer reaction networks.
summary: This paper establishes a quantum circuit framework to simulate polymerization kinetics by encoding the non-unitary rate matrix into a unitary quantum operation. By developing explicit block encodings using sparse-oracle and LCU methods, the authors achieve an exponential memory reduction, demonstrating a path toward simulating high-dimensional chemical reaction networks on quantum hardware.
main_problem: Simulating the complex, exponentially growing state space of polymer polymerization kinetics using quantum computation.
main_result: The authors developed concrete quantum circuit foundations using block encodings (Sparse-Oracle and LCU) that achieve an exponential memory saving of O(log N) qubits relative to the system size N.
method: They encode the non-unitary rate matrix A governing the kinetics into a sub-block of a larger unitary operator, utilizing techniques like sparse-oracle constructions and Linear Combination of Unitaries (LCU) decomposition.
model_or_system: The system models polymerization kinetics, specifically single-monomer (Model A) and two-monomer copolymerization (Model B), governed by linear ODEs (du/dt = Au). The state space grows exponentially with chain length.
key_observables: Reproduced classical time evolution for reactivity ratios; resource estimates (qubit counts, gate counts) for the encoding circuit.
important_parameters: The matrix dimension N, the number of system qubits $n_{sys} = \lceil\log_2 Nceil$, and the gate counts scaling up to $10^4 - 10^5$ gates at $n_{sys} \sim 10^3$.
main_assumptions: The simulation is limited to linear kinetic equations (constant monomer concentration) and the encoding only addresses the matrix representation, not the full solver complexity.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the chain-growth process, the m-index labeling scheme, and circuit diagrams for the encoding oracles (e.g., Ocol for Model B).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical problem, details the mathematical formulation ($ rac{du}{dt} = A u$), develops and compares two encoding strategies (Sparse-Oracle vs. LCU) for Model A and Model B, validates the encodings via simulation, and concludes with resource analysis.
why_interesting: This work provides a direct, resource-estimated quantum circuit blueprint for simulating complex, high-dimensional chemical dynamics, which is a key application area for quantum simulation algorithms.
